title: Swarm Learning And Clinical Data: Evaluating The Benefit of a New Node For The Whole Network

sections.title: 研究问题
sections.text:

【Introduction · Par9】In this paper, we aim to address these questions by systematically evaluating the performance of SL under various data configurations across participating nodes. Our investigation focuses on analyzing how a swarm network adapts and performs when a newly introduced node contributes unique data that has not previously been utilized in the learning process of other nodes. In this setting, the expected performance improvement associated with additional homogeneous data is not the main focus of the study; rather, it represents the controlled condition under which the contribution of the new node can be isolated and interpreted. Through this analysis, we want to propose a framework for checking the adaptability and robustness of the SL framework in handling different data distributions with multiple datasets.

【Introduction · Par2】The clinical field has increasingly embraced digital technologies to improve patient care and, more broadly, to transform the management and experience of healthcare. Today, numerous hospitals and healthcare organizations utilize digital solutions, and some clinical datasets are accessible to researchers and healthcare professionals. Analyzing these datasets plays a crucial role in decision-making processes, such as resource allocation, patient care strategies, disease progression forecasting, and the development of treatment protocols [1].

sections.title: 研究方法
sections.text:
《Swarm Learning And Clinical Data: Evaluating The Benefit of a New Node For The Whole Network》：方法与研究设计的原文依据。

【Methodology · Par22】Thanks to its decentralized nature and emphasis on data privacy, the SL framework is well-suited for distributed healthcare analysis across multiple centers. Rather than focusing on SL’s security aspects, this study aims to evaluate its learning performance across various scenarios. In this section, we want to systematically analyze the effects of a single –new– node when it joins the swarm network, based on different data distributions between this node and all the others that were already part of the network. In particular, we want to analyze the impact of this new node on the swarm network, as well as the influence of this node on itself and the other nodes in terms of learning performance when different data distribution scenarios are considered. This analysis simulates different real-world situations in which the amount of data between centers differs. To do so, we considered this new node as a reference node with a given percentage of the training set, uniformly distributing the remaining part of it in the other nodes. Learning performance is evaluated by varying the percentage of the training set assigned to the new node, while evenly distributing the remaining portion across the other nodes. To ensure consistency in class representation, stratified sampling is used to maintain the target class distribution. This ensures that both target classes, including the less frequent sepsis class, remain represented across the different data splits according to their original proportions. However, several key factors may influence performance or must be considered to fully understand the causes of performance variation.

sections.title: 主要结果
sections.text:
《Swarm Learning And Clinical Data: Evaluating The Benefit of a New Node For The Whole Network》：结果的原文依据；数值与适用人群以引文为准。

【Results and Discussion · Par69】In the following, we will illustrate and discuss the results obtained through the analysis of a swarm network with up to 5 nodes, when a new node joined the network. First of all, we need to calculate our reference performance, that is, the average AUROC for the central model. The central model, as well as the swarm and local models, were tested on the same test set with unseen data. We used a model trained on a single server with the whole dataset resulting from all the single datasets of nodes in the network. That is, when the new node joins the network, we evaluate the central model only once with 100% of the training set available. In the scenarios where the new node is not present, we calculated the central model over the portion of the dataset given to the nodes. That is, with 3 other nodes with a 20% data split for each, we calculated the central model over their overall 60% of the dataset. The central model performance is evaluated by averaging five repetitions with random shuffles of the training data with different random seeds, and we obtained an AUC of 0.8567 for MIMIC-III, and 0.8828 for MIMIC-IV.

【Conclusions · Par90】In this paper, we analyzed the impact of a new node on an already existing swarm learning network. To measure this impact, we proposed, as an original contribution, seven different key performance indicators (KPIs) designed to characterize the effect of the new node on different components of the system: the new node itself, the overall swarm network, and the pre-existing nodes, considering performance, stability, fairness, and data-related aspects. We deliberately adopted two homogeneous ICU datasets (MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV) in order to evaluate the behavior of the proposed KPIs in a controlled setting, where the impact of the new node could be observed without the confounding influence of heterogeneity.

To measure this impact, we proposed, as an original contribution, seven different key performance indicators (KPIs) designed to characterize the effect of the new node on different components of the system: the new node itself, the overall swarm network, and the pre-existing nodes, considering performance, stability, fairness, and data-related aspects. 【HPE Swarm Learning Software · Par17】Hewlett-Packard Enterprise (HPE) developed a freely available SL software, named HPE Swarm Learning Community Edition1, that allows training collaborative models between different servers without sharing the training data. This is achieved by individual nodes sharing model weights derived from training the model on the local data of each node.

【HPE Swarm Learning Software · Par19】The SL process begins with enrollment on the swarm smart contract by each node. Next, nodes proceed to train a local copy of the model iteratively over multiple epochs, for a fixed number of iterations. After reaching the number of iterations, each node exports its model parameters and sends them to the epoch leader, which is chosen randomly at each synchronization step between all the nodes. The epoch leader merges all the models’ parameters from each node and sends the merged parameters to the other peers. Then, each node trains the model until the fixed iteration number is reached again. A final swarm model is obtained at the end of all the synchronization steps, and each node receives the swarm merged model.
